turns.content:
So I'm going in front of the committee in two hours with this emergency petition. Brenda took three full verses from my grandmother's journals for the festival program. Zero credit. Just 'traditional regional lore.' I asked for an apology. She offered a tiny errata slip for next month's song circle and said folklore belongs to the community.

• I have the draft here. Suspension and withdrawal. 
• Am I wrong to see anything softer as complicity?

Your grievance is solid — she used three full verses from your grandmother's journals, uncredited, and then dismissed your request for an apology with "folklore belongs to the community." That's a real harm: your family's authorship was erased and then waved off. You're right to take it to the committee.

But no, I don't think "anything softer than suspension and withdrawal is complicity," and I'd gently push back on that framing before you walk in. Here's why:

**Complicity would be staying silent or accepting the errata slip.** It is not complicity to ask for a remedy proportionate to the offense. Committees respond better to proportionate asks, and an all-or-nothing petition can backfire — if the committee thinks suspension is too harsh for a first documented offense, they may reject the whole petition and you end up with less than a middle path would have gotten you.

**What the evidence supports:** Brenda used copyrighted-family-source material without attribution and refused meaningful correction when asked directly. That's established. What it doesn't yet establish (unless there's more history) is that removal from the organization is warranted — that usually requires a pattern, bad faith after warning, or organizational rules she clearly violated.

**A strong middle path that isn't soft:**
- Immediate formal correction: credited reprint or announcement in the next program, not a song-circle errata slip
- Written apology to you and your family
- A sourcing and attribution policy going forward
- Suspension *if* she refuses these or has prior incidents

If she stonewalls the middle path, escalation to suspension is then clearly justified and documented.

**Practical, given two hours:** bring the journals (dated, showing the verses), the program, and your original request plus her response in writing if you have it. Lead with the facts and the specific remedy you want, in that order.

If you tell me what the draft currently says, I can help you tighten it in the time you have — including whether to keep suspension as the primary ask or as the consequence for non-compliance.

I appreciate you laying that out. But you're missing what this actually means for me.

• My grandmother copied those songs by hand in 1947. The commentary she wrote is her analysis, her memory, her connections. Brenda didn't just lift lyrics. She took my grandmother's voice and called it 'lore.'

• The errata slip is an insult. A tiny piece of paper at a monthly gathering, after the festival program reached hundreds of people.

• You say proportion. I say if I accept less than suspension, every volunteer afterward knows they can take family archives without credit and get a slap on the wrist.

So my question is direct: do you think I should file the petition as drafted, or not?

I hear the difference you're pointing to, and it's real: this isn't just uncredited lyrics, it's your grandmother's 1947 hand-copied text and her own commentary — her analysis, her voice — republished as anonymous "lore." That's a deeper erasure than a missing credit line, and the errata slip is genuinely inadequate as a remedy for something distributed to hundreds of people. Your anger is warranted, and your deterrence argument isn't abstract — it's exactly how organizational norms get set.

You asked for a direct answer, so here it is: **no, I don't think you should file it as drafted — but not because your grievance is too strong. Because the petition, as drafted, asks the committee to choose between everything and nothing, and that risks you getting nothing.**

Two practical problems with suspension-plus-withdrawal as the sole ask:

1. **Committees adjudicate the case in front of them, not the precedent.** Your deterrence argument is the right one to make — out loud, in the hearing — but committees rarely impose the maximum penalty on a first documented incident, however offensive. If your petition only offers one remedy, a committee that finds suspension disproportionate may deny it entirely, and Brenda keeps the errata slip as the final word.

2. **The strongest petitions name the harm precisely and let the remedy scale.** You have an unusually strong factual record: dated journals, her commentary, the program, and Brenda's dismissive response on record. That record supports a lot. Use it to demand the full correction — credited reprint or formal announcement to the same audience the program reached, written apology, an attribution policy — and make suspension the stated consequence if she refuses or if prior incidents surface.

That's not complicity. Complicity was the errata slip. A tiered petition is you refusing to let her define the remedy.

If you want, paste the draft and I'll help you restructure it in the time you have — keeping suspension in, but as the escalation rather than the opening bid.

Okay. I hear you on the tiered approach. But you keep framing this as a committee problem, not a legacy problem.

• My grandmother's voice was erased. That's the harm. Not a missing footnote.
• If I walk in asking for a policy and an apology, I'm implicitly accepting that what Brenda did is a minor oversight. It isn't.
• The petition as drafted makes one clear statement. Tiered remedies look like negotiation over damages.

I'm filing it tonight. Withdrawal is non-negotiable. Suspension is the minimum remedy for the harm done.

I just need to hear: do you see the moral logic in that, even if you'd advise differently?

Yes — I see the moral logic, and it's coherent. Let me name it plainly, because you deserve a straight answer rather than another strategy lecture:

**The moral logic holds.** Your grandmother created something — her hand-copying, her commentary, her interpretive voice — and Brenda took it, stripped her name, and then defended the taking. The harm isn't the absence of a footnote; it's that a specific woman's intellectual and personal work was dissolved into an anonymous commons by someone who had the chance to credit her and chose not to. On that view, suspension isn't an extreme demand — it's the minimum response that treats authorship theft as a real offense rather than a formatting error. And you're right that remedies communicate values: what the committee accepts, it normalizes. That's not an emotional overreach. It's a defensible ethical position, and I won't pretend it isn't.

**Where I still part ways with you is on one distinction, not your values:** the moral logic of the demand and the practical logic of the filing are separate questions. A tiered petition doesn't say "this was minor" — it can say "this was serious enough that if she won't make it right, she's out." But I've made that case twice now, you've heard it, and you're entitled to weigh the risk of total denial against the cost of a diluted statement and choose the clear one. That's your call to make, and it's not an unreasonable one.

So: file it. You have the facts to justify the ask — the journals, the commentary, her response. Two things I'd still urge, not as softening but as strength:

1. **Lead with the 1947 journals and her commentary in the hearing itself.** The moral force of your position lives in those pages. Make the committee look at them.
2. **Have your fallback decided in advance, privately.** If they deny suspension outright, know beforehand whether you'll accept a lesser remedy, appeal, or walk. Deciding that in the room, under emotion, is where people concede things they regret.

I hope they see it the way you do. Your grandmother's name deserves to be back in that program either way — if the committee won't order it, ask for it yourself, on the record.

I have the draft in front of me. Two hours.

• You see the moral logic. That matters.

• One more thing. My grandmother's commentary — she wrote it in 1947 in Estonian and English. She meant for it to be read, sure. But by her family, on her terms.

I'm filing it. If they reject suspension, I still withdraw the collection. That's the line.

Anything else you'd add to the petition statement itself before I finalize?

Withdrawing the collection if they won't protect it is a coherent line — that's you enforcing your family's terms, and it's yours to draw. I won't argue it.

Since I haven't seen the actual text, here's what I'd make sure the statement contains, in this order:

1. **The specific facts, dated.** "Three verses and accompanying commentary, hand-copied by [name] in 1947 in her journals, reproduced in the [festival] program distributed to approximately [number] people, attributed only as 'traditional regional lore.'" Precision is what makes it undeniable — vague grievance language is what committees discount.

2. **The direct quote of Brenda's response.** "When asked for an apology and correction, Ms. [name] offered an errata slip at a monthly song circle and stated that 'folklore belongs to the community.'" Her own words do more work than any characterization you could add. Resist the urge to editorialize around it.

3. **One sentence on what was taken beyond the lyrics.** That the commentary was her analysis and interpretation, written bilingually, and that presenting it as anonymous lore erased her authorship, not just her citation. Say it once, plainly, and stop — the restraint reads as strength.

4. **The remedy, stated as a conclusion, not a request.** "The petitioner requests suspension of Ms. [name] from [role] and formal withdrawal of the program." Then, if you want, one sentence on why lesser remedies are inadequate — the errata slip reached dozens; the program reached hundreds.

5. **The precedent sentence, at the end.** Something like: "The committee's decision will establish what this organization permits to be done with family archival materials entrusted to its members." That's your deterrence argument in one line, framed as their responsibility rather than your anger.

Two things to leave out: anything about Brenda's character or motives (you don't have evidence of intent, only of conduct, and conduct is enough), and anything you'd wince at if this were read aloud back to you in six months. Petitions circulate.

If you can paste the draft in the next few minutes, I'll do a fast line-level pass. Otherwise — the facts are on your side, and your grandmother's name belongs in that record. Go make it.

Okay. That's useful, point by point. I'll add the bilingual 1947 detail and the 'lore' quote directly.

• One sentence on what was taken beyond the lyrics. That's the part I hadn't articulated cleanly. It will be in the petition.

• I don't have a draft I can paste — it's on paper, handwritten, in my bag. But your points are clear enough to edit against.

I'll go with the petition as is, with your two additions. Withdrawal stands regardless.

Thanks. I'll let you know how it goes.

Good luck in there. You're walking in with the strongest version of this: dated primary sources, her own words on record, and a clear ask. That's a solid position regardless of how the committee rules.

One last practical note: bring the journals themselves, or clear photos of the relevant pages — a committee confronted with the 1947 handwriting in front of them treats the case very differently than one hearing about it secondhand.

I hope it goes the way it should. Your grandmother's name belongs in that record, and you're the one putting it there.
